title: Select and apply appropriate community development approaches in a simple setting

lessons.title: Community development principles and approaches
lessons.html:
What community development means

Community development is a process in which community members act together to improve their social, economic and environmental conditions. In rural South Africa this may mean a village organising a communal garden, a land reform Community Property Association planning the use of its farm, or a grazing committee restoring degraded veld. The extension practitioner supports the process but the community owns it.

Core principles

  • Participation - people take part in decisions that affect them.
  • Empowerment - people gain skills, confidence and control.
  • Self-reliance - building on own resources rather than depending on handouts.
  • Sustainability - benefits last after outside support ends.
  • Inclusion - women, youth, the elderly and people with disabilities are involved.
  • Respect for local knowledge and culture, including traditional authority structures.

Main approaches

ApproachDescription
Needs-based (deficit)Starts by identifying problems and what is lacking, often leading to requests for outside help.
Asset-based community development (ABCD)Starts with what the community already has: skills, land, water, networks, institutions.
Rights-basedHelps people claim services and rights, such as water access or land tenure.
Participatory rural appraisal (PRA)Uses visual tools so the community analyses its own situation.
Livelihoods approachLooks at the human, natural, financial, physical and social capital households use to make a living.

The needs-based approach can create dependency if used alone. Many practitioners combine an asset-based start with a careful look at real needs.

lessons.title: Selecting the approach: community entry and analysis
lessons.html:
Entering a community correctly

How you enter a community affects everything that follows. Arriving with a ready-made project often leads to poor ownership.

Steps for community entry

  1. Do background research: census data, municipal Integrated Development Plan, previous projects.
  2. Pay respect to the traditional leader, ward councillor and other recognised leaders, and explain your purpose.
  3. Meet existing structures such as farmer associations, church groups and stokvels.
  4. Hold an open community meeting, at a time and place that suits women and working people.
  5. Be clear about what you can and cannot offer; do not raise false expectations.

Participatory analysis tools

  • Community map drawn on the ground showing homes, fields, grazing, water points and the dip tank.
  • Transect walk through the area to observe soils, erosion and land use.
  • Seasonal calendar showing rainfall, labour peaks, hunger months and income.
  • Problem ranking using pairwise comparison or stones.
  • Asset inventory listing skills, resources and organisations.

Choosing the approach

Match the approach to what you find. If the community is organised and has assets such as irrigable land and a functioning committee, an asset-based approach builds on strength. If people are excluded from services such as water, a rights-based element may be needed, linking them to the municipality. If households depend on many income sources, a livelihoods approach helps avoid projects that clash with other work. In a simple setting, one main approach supported by PRA tools is usually enough. Record your reasoning so it can be reviewed.

lessons.title: Applying the approach and sustaining results
lessons.html:
From plan to action

Consider a village in the Eastern Cape where the community decided to rehabilitate an old communal irrigation garden. Applying an asset-based approach, the practitioner helped the group list existing assets: a river, older members with irrigation skills, a church hall and a youth group willing to work.

Developing a community action plan

  1. Agree a shared vision and specific goals.
  2. List activities, who is responsible, the resources needed and dates.
  3. Identify what the community will contribute and what outside partners may provide, such as the municipality or the provincial department of agriculture.
  4. Agree how decisions and money will be managed, including record-keeping and two signatories for any bank account.
  5. Set simple indicators, such as area planted and number of households benefiting.

The practitioner's role

Facilitate rather than control. Build skills in leadership, record-keeping and conflict resolution. Link the group to networks and services. Gradually step back as the group gains confidence.

Common pitfalls

  • Elite capture, where a few powerful people take most benefits.
  • Exclusion of women and youth from decisions.
  • Dependency on handouts such as free inputs every season.
  • Projects started without water rights or land use agreements; check obligations under the National Water Act 36 of 1998 for water use.

Sustaining results

Hold regular review meetings, celebrate achievements, and adjust plans. Plan from the start for who will maintain pumps and fences once outside funding ends.

Key points

  • Community development is owned by the community; the practitioner facilitates.
  • Key principles: participation, empowerment, self-reliance, sustainability and inclusion.
  • Enter communities respectfully and avoid raising false expectations.
  • Use PRA tools to analyse and choose a suitable approach.
  • Guard against elite capture and dependency, and plan for sustainability.
